inflection_points.summary: fix: a claimed candidate was stored as never-checked, so it was checked forever
inflection_points.body:
Self-review of the TTL two commits back. The claim branch upserted `cand`
before with_linked_prs had been applied, so every candidate rejected as
claimed went into the table with open_pr_count NULL.

Two things wrong with that. Candidate's own docstring defines NULL there as
"the timeline was never read, never that there are no PRs" -- and we had read
it, and found the assignee's own pull request. And recent_pr_check requires a
non-NULL count precisely because a NULL one is not evidence of a check, so
every claimed candidate was re-read on every sweep: the exact per-sweep cost
the TTL exists to remove, left in place for the rows LEAST likely to have
changed, since a bounty already awarded is the one thing that stays awarded.

The test that was supposed to catch this passed for the wrong reason. It
queued no timeline response, so the attempted call raised an unqueued-request
error, which stage 3 caught as an ordinary timeline failure, warned about,
and skipped the upsert for -- leaving the claim standing by accident and the
assertion green. It now asserts no timeline URL was requested at all and that
no timeline warning reached the digest, and was verified red against the old
code before this fix was kept.

The failed-read test was weak in the same way: the candidate had never been
stored at all, so it exercised nothing about the stamp. It now checks a
successfully-stamped row whose TTL has expired, fails the re-read, asserts
the stamp did NOT advance, and asserts the very next sweep asks again rather
than sitting out a fresh six-hour window on the strength of a failure.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the staleness rule only ever judged what it had just discovered
inflection_points.body:
149f5c0/1d5852d gave the comment ceiling a retroactive half. e785fef gave
the staleness rule none, so a row that went idle AFTER being stored stayed
live indefinitely -- until a source happened to rediscover it, which for a
months-old bounty is never.

The argument is stronger here than for the ceiling, not weaker. A stale issue
is by definition one nothing is happening to, and BountyLabelSource sorts by
`updated` -- so the stalest rows are exactly the ones its pages reach last
and its stop() reaches never. The rule that most needed a retroactive pass
was the only one without one.

store.apply_staleness mirrors apply_comment_ceiling, comparing GitHub's own
timestamp format lexicographically (fixed width, always UTC, so string order
IS chronological). The cutoff is days+1 because free_reject rejects on
`idle > days` and timedelta.days truncates, putting the real line at eight
whole days for STALE_AFTER_DAYS=7; a test pins 7.9 / 8.0 / 8.1 days against
free_reject's own verdict on the same rows, because a rule that keeps a
candidate at stage 1 and rejects it retroactively on the same sweep is worse
than either answer alone. An empty updated_at is skipped rather than swept
up: it sorts before every real timestamp, and "I do not know when" must not
read as "a long time ago".

The reason no longer interpolates the measured idle count. "no activity in
221d" gave every candidate a different spelling of one verdict, and the board
groups its reject table by exact string while clear_rejections matches by
exact string -- so the biggest rule on the board could only ever appear as
dozens of one-row reasons nobody could see the size of or reverse. Both paths
now call filters.stale_reason(), which is also what made writing the SQL half
possible at all: it judges in bulk and has no per-row count to interpolate.

inflection_points.summary: fix: two Expensify calls spent more quota than they had reserved
inflection_points.body:
The reservation guard is the thing standing between a throttle and a digest
that reports the world as empty (HANDOFF.md trap #3), so a request it has not
counted is a hole in it. Two of them:

_standing reserved ONE search unit and then called search_issues with
max_pages=EXPENSIFY_STANDING_MAX_PAGES (4). Two requests are actually made
today -- 83 results at SEARCH_PER_PAGE 50 -- and the cap is 4 precisely
because that number grows. Every other caller in the tree already reserves up
front: BountyLabelSource reserves self.max_pages, known_payers reserves
`pages`, ever_closed_with reserves 2 for its 2 requests.

The event poll reserved one CORE unit for the whole call, while
poll_label_events' deep-paging block calls _get up to EVENT_MAX_PAGES-1 extra
times. It now reserves the cap when a watermark exists and one when it does
not, because since_event_id is what switches that block on -- reserving five
without a watermark would be spending the guard on requests that cannot
happen. Live as of the previous commit, which is the first time that block
ever ran.

inflection_points.summary: fix: silence had come to mean five things, and none of them said which
inflection_points.body:
main() passes notify_when_empty=False for both jobs, which is right -- 144
"nothing new" messages a day trains the reader to ignore the channel, so the
one that matters lands somewhere nobody looks. But `flock -n` exits 1 and
prints NOTHING, so Discord silence became indistinguishable between a healthy
quiet market, a hung job holding its lock, a dead box, a lost .env and a
removed crontab. That is the collision this codebase exists to prevent,
reintroduced one layer out.

Two halves, because a log and a channel answer different questions.

The cron jobs now leave a line when they skip. -E 99 and a `[ $? -eq 99 ]`
test rather than a bare `|| echo`: flock passes the command's own exit status
through when it DID get the lock, so the simple form would file every python
traceback as a lock conflict -- one wrong story swapped for another. Verified
locally against a real flock in all three states: lock held writes the line,
lock free does not, and a command exiting 3 does not.

The digest now speaks once every HEARTBEAT_S (24h) regardless, carrying the
sweep count and the live totals. Periodic, not per-run: at ten-minute sweeps
that is 1 message in 144, and the branch is tested against two hours of
sweeps producing exactly two beats rather than twelve. The sweep COUNT is
what makes a half-dead deployment visible -- a heartbeat reading 6 where 144
belong is a watch cron that has stopped, said out loud by the digest cron
that has not.

Stored in http_cache the way board-signature is, and advanced only by a beat
that actually reached someone. A recorded-but-undelivered beat would buy
another full day of silence out of a delivery failure, which is exactly what
it exists to break; --dry-run does not spend it either.

Also corrected the installer's flock preflight comment, which still said both
jobs share one lock. They stopped four commits ago.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the deep paging added last commit had never run once
inflection_points.body:
poll_help_wanted_events returns events already filtered to `labeled` + Help
Wanted + not-a-PR -- a tiny minority of the feed. The caller then took its
watermark from THAT list, which breaks in both directions and both were live:

  * no matching event yet -> no watermark ever written -> since_event_id
    stays None -> the paging block is skipped entirely. That is the deployed
    state: measured 2026-08-10, the newest Help Wanted label event on
    Expensify/App was three days old, so the feature shipped inert;
  * after one matching event -> the watermark freezes at that id until
    another Help Wanted label lands, so every poll in between re-pages the
    full EVENT_MAX_PAGES (5 core calls, every ten minutes) to re-read pages
    it had already read.

poll_label_events is the only function that sees the unfiltered payload, so
it now returns the newest id ON THE PAGE as a fourth value rather than
leaving the caller to reconstruct it from output it cannot reconstruct it
from. None means the page said nothing -- empty, or a 304 -- and is
deliberately not 0, which is a real id every event compares greater than.

payer-watch unpacks and DISCARDS it, with a note saying why: passing
since_event_id is what turns deep paging on, and that loop runs across up to
WATCH_MAX_REPOS (60) repos a sweep, where one page each is what makes
watching them affordable at all.

Nothing in the suite mentioned since_event_id, watermark or EVENT_MAX_PAGES.
Eleven tests now do, including both failure directions above, the stop at
the page that reaches the watermark, the stop at the cap when it never does,
and the single page read when there is no watermark to page toward.

inflection_points.summary: fix: two modules agreed on a string by convention, and nothing checked
inflection_points.body:
store.PAYOUT_REJECT_PREFIXES was a tuple of hand-typed literals, matched with
SQL LIKE against reasons built as f-strings in payers.payout_reject. Two
copies of the same words in two modules, linked by nothing.

A reword on either side raises nothing. bounty_inventory silently stops
counting those rows, the repo's advertised inventory falls back under
UNPAID_REPO_THRESHOLD, the rule abstains, and the survivors look exactly like
a repo that was never suspicious -- which is the self-erosion bug
bounty_inventory exists to fix, restored with no error anywhere. Measured
2026-08-10, that erosion took SecureBananaLabs/bug-bounty from 31 live rows
to 3 in a single sweep, three being under the threshold of ten.

There was no test naming bounty_inventory, algora_repos or
PAYOUT_REJECT_PREFIXES at all.

payers now owns the strings and BUILDS its reasons from them, so there is one
string used twice rather than two strings expected to agree; store imports
them lazily, as it already does for the rest of payers.

Three tests, because the coupling has three halves worth holding:

  * every reason payout_reject can return, enumerated by driving all three
    rejecting branches, asserted against the prefix set -- two of three
    passing is the shape of this bug, not a defence against it;
  * an ast walk over payout_reject itself, so a FOURTH reason added later
    cannot quietly fall out of the LIKE. Verified it fails on an added
    branch before being kept;
  * the behaviour the functions exist for: a payout-rejected row still counts
    toward its repo's advertised inventory (a fork rejection does not), and a
    repo where any one row wears the Algora label is flagged for all of them
    -- the 28-rejected/3-survived split measured on the same repo.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the ten-minute job re-read 83 timelines it had already read
inflection_points.body:
Expensify's standing search returns every open Help Wanted issue on every
sweep. Measured 2026-08-10: all 83 survive free_reject -- Expensify is in
ASSIGNEE_NOT_A_CLAIM, so the assignee rule that drops them everywhere else
never fires -- survive repo_reject, and reach stage 3. Stage 3 had no cache,
no dedup against rows it had already judged and no per-source cap, so each
one cost 1-3 core calls plus CORE_CALL_PAUSE_S (0.5s), every time.

WATCH_SOURCES puts that on the TEN-MINUTE cron: 1.5-2.5 minutes of wall
clock per sweep and 500-1500 guard-counted core units an hour, against a
guard that refuses to start a run once 3500 of the 5000/hr pool is spent. It
fitted inside ten minutes by luck rather than by construction, and `flock -n`
turns an overrun into a silently skipped cycle -- which is indistinguishable
from a healthy quiet market.

candidates.pr_checked_at records when the timeline was actually READ, added
through ADDED_COLUMNS the way open_pr_count was. recent_pr_check() returns
the stored verdict only while it is younger than TIMELINE_RECHECK_S, and
returns None -- go and look -- for no row, no stamp, a stamp too old, or a
NULL count, because every candidate rejected before stage 3 carries a NULL
count and a row existing is not evidence anyone read its timeline.

Six hours, and it is a trade, not a free win: a claim can land at any moment,
so a reused verdict can show a bounty awarded five hours ago. That is the
same safe direction TIMELINE_MAX_PAGES already takes -- a kept candidate gets
read by a human who sees the assigned PR, a rejected one disappears unseen.
Six rather than three so a watch sweep is not forced to redo the standing
list between digests, rather than twenty-four so a claim never survives more
than two digests. 83 x 4 checks a day against 12,000-36,000.

Three things the reuse gets right or it would be worse than the bug:

  * a candidate never checked is checked immediately, whatever the TTL --
    the label-event path is as fast as it ever was;
  * the stored open_pr_count is reused, so the score does not quietly become
    "uncontested" on the sweep that skips;
  * the CLAIM is carried forward with it. Stage 3's verdict is two facts, and
    reusing only the count would rewrite a claimed candidate with
    rejected=NULL and put an awarded bounty back on the board with no call
    made to blame it on. CLAIM_PREFIX exists so the writer and the reader of
    that reason cannot drift apart.

A read that FAILED writes no stamp at all: recording one would suppress the
retry for a whole six-hour window, which is "I could not look" wearing the
face of "I looked".

inflection_points.summary: fix: the watch was starved by the digest, and one page was a bet on a quiet repo
inflection_points.body:
Two reasons the Expensify channel has produced zero candidates.

The locks. I gave both cron jobs the SAME flock hours earlier. A full sweep
spends ~20 minutes in the timeline stage alone -- twice the watch job's entire
interval -- so every digest starved two to four watch cycles. That is exactly
backwards: the watch is the time-critical one, because its whole purpose is to
catch a label before it rolls off the events page, while a skipped digest just
reports the same inventory three hours later. One lock per job now. The shared
SQLite file, which the single lock was reaching for, is already handled a layer
down by timeout=30 and upsert_candidate's hardening.

The paging. poll_label_events read exactly one 100-event page, which is a bet
that the repo is quiet. Measured 2026-08-10 on Expensify/App that page covered
27 MINUTES against a 10-minute poll; the day before it covered 2h52m. A 6x swing
in velocity, and losing the bet is silent -- the label is simply never seen.

It now pages until it reaches an event id it has already passed. A WATERMARK,
not a per-event seen-test: only a matching label is ever recorded as handled and
those are a tiny minority of the feed, so a seen-test would recognise nothing
and page the full cap every poll. Event ids increase monotonically, so 'we have
reached an id we already passed' is the honest stopping point.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the comment ceiling has to reach the rows already stored
inflection_points.body:
free_reject only judges candidates a source hands over this sweep, and a
months-old bounty may never be rediscovered. Measured 2026-08-10, 36 live rows
were already past the ceiling when it shipped -- without this they would have
sat on the board forever while the rule applied to new inventory only.

Same reason apply_dismissals and apply_payout_rejections exist, and the reason
string is built to match free_reject's exactly so the board's reject table
groups both paths under one row instead of showing one rule twice.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the payout rule was erasing the condition it fires on
inflection_points.body:
Two leaks, both visible in the published board, both structural rather than
threshold-tuning.

A repo's ledger is a fact about the REPO, but check_rewarded was keyed on the
labels of whichever issue was in hand. Measured 2026-08-10: 28 of
SecureBananaLabs/bug-bounty's candidates carried 💎 Bounty and were rejected on
a zero rewarded count, while three siblings tagged only ['bug', 'good first
issue', 'bounty', '$1.2k'] survived the same sweep -- one repo, one ledger, two
verdicts, decided by tagging. algora_repos() answers it per repo instead.

And UNPAID_REPO_THRESHOLD was measured against currently-live rows, so the rule
shrank its own basis as it worked. SecureBananaLabs fell 31 -> 3 live in one
sweep; 3 is under the threshold of 10, so the next sweep abstained and the
survivors became permanently untouchable. bounty-plaza did the same at 2. A
filter that destroys its own trigger stops firing, and what it leaves behind is
indistinguishable from a repo that was never suspicious.

bounty_inventory() counts live rows PLUS the ones the payout rules themselves
rejected, because 'is this repo advertising a pile of bounties' is a question
about the repo, not about how many of its issues survived our filters. Other
rejections -- forks, below-floor, archived -- are deliberately not counted back:
those say the candidate was never worth ranking, not that the repo does not pay.

inflection_points.summary: fix: Algora's own ledger outranks a ratio, and a ratio needs a sample
inflection_points.body:
Farms held 11 of the top 15 slots by score on the live box today. Three
separate holes, none of them the ratio rule failing:

  repo                        live   rewarded   closed 💎   with PR
  SecureBananaLabs/bug-bounty   31          0           1         1
  UnsafeLabs/Bounty-Hunters      9          0           0         0
  Spectral-Finance/lux           2          0           0         0

SecureBananaLabs passed because 1/1 is 100%. A ratio on a sample of one is not
evidence. UnsafeLabs was never judged at all: nine live candidates, one under
UNPAID_REPO_THRESHOLD, so the gate abstained before any rule ran.

Both wear Algora's own 💎 Bounty label and have never had a single issue marked
💰 Rewarded. That is not an inference from the payer roster -- which is a sample
of the 43 most-recent payers, and weak by construction -- it is Algora's own
record for that repo saying nobody was ever paid. So rewarded_count reads the
repo directly and its verdict does not wait for the open-count threshold.

It is asked ONLY of repos wearing the exact Algora label. microg/GmsCore has
14,170 stars, a real $1,340 bounty and 0 rewarded, because it never opted into
Algora at all -- absence of the label is absence of a record to be silent about,
and that asymmetry is what makes skipping the threshold safe.

The ratio now needs CLOSED_SAMPLE_MIN closures before it is trusted, and below
that it ABSTAINS rather than rejects. The direction is the point:
commaai/opendbc is a genuine payer with seven closed bounties, and rejecting a
short track record would kill exactly what this tool exists to find.

apply_payout_rejections loses its own copy of the gate -- the third -- which
carried the same nine-under-ten hole for rows already in the table.

inflection_points.summary: fix: one issue's timeline could consume a whole sweep
inflection_points.body:
Measured 2026-08-10 on the live box, mid-deploy: core spend went 195 -> 270,
seventy-five consecutive calls in ninety seconds, while open_pr_count did not
advance by a single row. Stage 3 was paging one issue's timeline -- 7,500+
events -- with nothing bounding it. Throughput fell to about three candidates a
minute, which over 975 survivors is longer than the interval of the cron that
calls it, and the run would have exhausted CORE_BUDGET_PER_RUN long before
finishing.

has_open_linked_pr could not hit this. It stopped at the first open PR and
almost never left page one. Counting removed that stop and nothing replaced the
bound; the recorded fixture has 167 events, so no test could see it either.

Paging now stops at TIMELINE_MAX_PAGES (3 = 300 events, which covers every real
bounty issue) and LinkedPRs.complete says whether the whole timeline was read.
Truncation is safe in both directions, which is what makes a cap acceptable
here: a claimant found is positive evidence and still rejects, and a claimant
not found leaves the candidate live -- the safe error, because a kept candidate
gets read by a human while a rejected one disappears.

Also un-fragiles the gist-token fallback test, which reloaded config and so read
the developer's real .env. It passed everywhere until the credential was
actually configured, then failed for a reason unrelated to the code.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the two cron jobs share a database and neither is as short as its schedule
inflection_points.body:
Measured 2026-08-10: a full sweep of 975 survivors spends about twenty minutes
in the timeline stage alone, one core call per candidate. That is twice the
watch job's entire interval, so the 10-minute sweep was starting on top of a
running digest and both were writing the same SQLite file.

The watch job is not cheap any more either. It was affordable because
/issues/events revalidates and a 304 costs nothing, but since the payout rules
landed it also clears stale rejections and can run paced searches of its own on
every invocation.

Both jobs now take the same flock. -n rather than -w: a sweep that cannot get
the lock skips, because queueing would build a backlog of sweeps racing to
report the same inventory and the next run is only minutes away.

The installer gained a preflight for flock itself. A crontab calling a missing
binary would fail every sweep with 127 into a log nobody reads, and a tracker
that reports nothing looks exactly like a market with nothing in it.

inflection_points.summary: fix: closing a bounty is not paying one, and a farm bulk-closes
inflection_points.body:
The label-agnostic payout rule rejected a repo only when it had NEVER closed an
issue carrying its bounty label. Verified against live data today, that is fooled
by the exact repo it was written for: zhangjiayang6835-cyber/bounty-plaza reports
198 closed 'Bounty' issues, so the rule abstained and 22 of its issues sat live
in the digest holding the top five slots by score.

Those closures are not payouts. Issues #12, #13 and #16 were closed at
10:43:51Z, :55Z and :58Z on 2026-07-12 -- seven seconds apart, none assigned, one
of them titled '[bounty][funding-pending]'. It is a bulk close, and closing costs
a farm nothing.

What separates them is whether the closure carried merged work. Measured:

    repo                     closed   with a linked PR   ratio
    bounty-plaza (farm)         198                 23     12%
    activepieces/activepieces   173                170     98%
    commaai/opendbc               7                  4     57%

A real programme closes a bounty BECAUSE a pull request landed. So the rule now
asks for both numbers and rejects below a third, which keeps opendbc -- seven
closed bounties, no Algora label, its own programme -- and drops the farm.

Note for the next person: GitHub's search API silently IGNORES -no:assignee. It
returned the identical 198 for a repo whose closed issues have no assignee at
all. 'linked:pr' does work.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the gist needs a scope the read token deliberately does not have
inflection_points.body:
Measured 2026-08-10 against the live API: GITHUB_TOKEN is a classic PAT with an
EMPTY scope list. That is exactly right for everything else this tool does --
it reads public issues and can do nothing else, so losing it costs nothing --
but creating or updating a gist needs the `gist` scope, and POST /gists answers
404 with it. GitHub reports a missing scope as not-found rather than forbidden,
so an under-scoped credential is indistinguishable from a deleted gist.

The board's credential is therefore separate rather than widening the read
token: BOUNTY_GIST_TOKEN, falling back to GITHUB_TOKEN so one sufficiently
scoped token still works. Least privilege -- one narrow token that can write one
gist, and a read token that stays powerless.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the silence rule was dead code on every real invocation
inflection_points.body:
run() defaults notify_when_empty=True so the test suite can assert on a digest
without wiring a fake channel. main() never passed anything else, so
`nothing_to_say and not notify_when_empty` was `True and False` every time the
cron ran and the branch was unreachable.

So the watch sweep had been posting to Discord every ten minutes whether or not
anything changed -- 144 messages a day, which is precisely the failure the rule
was written to prevent. The comment above it has been describing behaviour the
code never had.

The new test asserts the wiring rather than the rule; the rule already has
test_a_quiet_watch_sweep_says_nothing.

inflection_points.summary: fix: three small ways a number or a name silently meant nothing
inflection_points.body:
* ASSIGNEE_NOT_A_CLAIM was not case-normalised, unlike PAID_LABELS three
  sections above it. `ASSIGNEE_NOT_A_CLAIM=Expensify` in .env -- the
  obvious spelling, since that is how the project writes its own name --
  would have matched no source, restored the blanket assignee reject,
  and taken the whole $250 channel dark again with no error anywhere.
  That is the exact failure this branch exists to fix, reintroduced by a
  capital letter. Lowered on both sides, with a test.

* test_score.py had no boundary case at stars=20, repo_age_days=90 or
  repo_open_issues=200. The three comparisons are deliberately
  asymmetric (>=, <, >) and bounty-plaza's measured 5 / 32 / 526 sits
  clear of all of them, so nothing pinned the edges and a later reader
  tuning FEW_STARS could not tell which side of each line the boundary
  falls on.

* tools/record_fixtures.py claimed the recorded timeline carries 6 open
  pull-request cross-references. Counted from the committed fixture it
  carries 29 (34 including closed), across 167 events and two pages --
  the 6 was measured before linked_pr_state() read past page 1 and never
  re-measured, directly contradicting the note underneath it. It also
  pointed at "Step 6" of a plan that has nine of them. Folded into one
  note that says what produced the number.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the board's headline numbers were page sizes, and its change signal died on day one
inflection_points.body:
Five defects, one cause: a page was being reported as an inventory.

* signature() counted len(rows) from a list capped at
  BOARD_UNRANKABLE_N (600). The true unrankable set is 934 post-revive
  (529 + 405), so the count pinned at 600 on the first sweep and never
  moved again -- has_changed's percentage arm was dead from day one and
  only the new-repo arm still worked. It now takes the count from the
  database. `repos` stays page-derived on purpose: the page is ordered
  first_seen_at DESC, so a NEW repo cannot be truncated away, and a repo
  falling off the tail is the case has_changed deliberately leaves to
  the count.

* The board-signature cache advanced even when publishing failed, and on
  --dry-run. A 40% move on a sweep where publish() raised was warned
  about and then FORGOTTEN: the next successful sweep compared against
  the advanced signature, saw nothing, and sent no link, so the move was
  never announced on any future sweep. It now advances only when a url
  came back.

* "Rankable — 25" over 48 priced live rows, fed DIGEST_TOP_N with no
  truncation notice, and `live 30` in the footer -- a sum of two capped
  lists that also double-counts a new top-scoring row -- while 982 rows
  were live. Counts now come from store.live_counts (one query, three
  honest numbers), the board has its own BOARD_RANKABLE_N, and a
  truncated section says "showing N of M". config's claim that "the
  footer says when it truncates" was false and is now true of the
  heading.

* An unset BOUNTY_GIST_ID warned on stderr only, because publish()
  returns None rather than raising. In Discord "the gist was never
  configured" and "the board did not move" were the same silence -- the
  collision publish()'s own docstring forbids -- and unset is the state
  both hosts deploy in. It now reaches the digest, and the deploy smoke
  test names it beside DISCORD_WEBHOOK.

  One deviation from the review, deliberately: the note is excluded from
  the silence test. It is a permanent configuration state, not news
  about this sweep, and letting it force delivery would be 144 identical
  messages a day out of the watch cron -- the failure the silence rule
  exists to prevent, arriving through the warning channel instead.

* The Rejected section rendered counts only, against design section D's
  "up to three example issues each". A count says a filter is BIG; an
  example says it is WRONG, and the example is the half that catches the
  next 'open linked PR = 562'.

clear_rejections' comment claimed revived rows are "put back in front of
the new one". They are not: run() judges only what a source rediscovers
this sweep. Corrected in both hunt.py and store.py, with why it is
acceptable -- all 446 revived rows carry score IS NULL, so they sort
last and cannot pollute the digest.

inflection_points.summary: fix: one throttled farm check could stall a whole sweep for hours
inflection_points.body:
ever_closed_with writes its cache only on success. A throttle or an
exception left nothing behind, and hunt's stage 1 -- unlike
apply_payout_rejections, which memoises None in its own closed_cache --
re-asked per candidate.

The cost is not one call. Measured against the live database: clearing
'open linked PR' revives 446 rows, taking live from 536 to 982 and repos
over UNPAID_REPO_THRESHOLD from 4 to 14. One of those repos holds 296
candidates, another 185. ever_closed_with called search_issues without
retries=, inheriting the 3-attempt 60/120/240s ladder, and because a
single-page search has no items in hand _fetch_search_page sleeps the
full 420s and then raises. 296 uncached asks at 420s is a 3-hourly sweep
that never finishes, a 10-minute watch cron piling up overlapping
processes, and no digest to say why.

Three changes:

* hunt.run memoises closed_for for the whole run, failures included. A
  None means "already asked, could not tell" -- an answer, cached like
  any other.
* ever_closed_with passes retries=0. The ladder exists because
  abandoning a DISCOVERY page cost 420 of 520 candidates; abandoning a
  farm check costs one abstain on one repo.
* ever_closed_with paces itself by SEARCH_PAGE_PAUSE_S. search_issues
  only pauses between pages and this asks for exactly one, so the 14
  calls apply_payout_rejections now makes went out back to back --
  against a burst guard measured tripping at ten (23 of 30 primary units
  still unspent).

payout_reject's first four conditions move to payers.label_to_check,
used by both call sites, so the gate that decides whether to spend a
search unit is not a hand-copied duplicate of the gate that decides the
verdict. A drifted copy is asymmetric: more permissive only wastes
quota, more restrictive passes closed=None where a count was needed and
silently keeps a farm. Same shape as 441d2ed.

The suite could not see any of this: conftest's no_budget_waiting zeroes
SEARCH_MAX_RETRIES and SEARCH_RETRY_BACKOFF_S. The regression test asks
instead how MANY times a failing closed_for is called -- once per (repo,
label), not once per candidate.

inflection_points.summary: fix: close three review findings in the board/gist wiring
inflection_points.body:
1. tests/test_hunt.py's dry_run=False sites called hunt.run() -> board.publish()
   with no injectable seam, and were only safe because this worktree's .env has
   BOUNTY_GIST_ID unset. The moment an operator configures a real gist, every
   local `pytest` run would PATCH it with test fixtures. Extended the existing
   board-sandbox autouse fixture to also force BOUNTY_GIST_ID empty, mirroring
   the GITHUB_TOKEN override already at the top of conftest.py -- and added the
   missing hunt.run() integration test covering the write/publish/link/cache
   round-trip, with board.publish and notify.send replaced wholesale.

2. The board block ran after notify.format_digest(), so a write or publish
   failure landed in `warnings` too late to reach the delivered digest, and the
   stderr print was gated on the id being unset -- a configured gist that
   failed for any other reason produced no stderr line either. Moved the board
   block before format_digest() so its warnings render into the same digest,
   and made the stderr print unconditional with a reason chosen per failure
   mode, mirroring the existing digest-delivery failure handling.

3. board._headers() duplicated github_api._headers() minus its User-Agent.
   Deleted the copy; both gist calls now use the shared one.

Also: corrected board.py's module docstring (create_gist/publish are not
pure), documented why has_changed's new-repo-vs-count asymmetry is
deliberate, and pinned the > (not >=) threshold behaviour with a test.

inflection_points.summary: fix: the stage-1 payout guard must abstain on an empty roster too
inflection_points.body:
Review caught a bug carried over verbatim from the brief: the stage-1 guard
in hunt.py checked "off the payer roster" and "over threshold" before calling
closed_for, but not "the roster was actually fetched". When known_payers
fails and returns an empty set -- deliberately, so payout_reject abstains
rather than treating "could not look" as "nobody pays" -- every repo is
vacuously "not in payer_repos", so the guard fired for every qualifying
candidate and payout_reject discarded every answer anyway (its first check is
`if not payers: return None`). Worse than wasted: reserve_or_wait blocks for
up to BUDGET_WAIT_S (65s) once the search pool is spent, and the roster fetch
usually fails from that same rate pressure, so a run could stall for minutes
buying answers already guaranteed to be thrown away.

Added `payer_repos and` to the guard, matching store.apply_payout_rejections,
which already got this right. Added test_an_empty_roster_never_reaches_closed_for,
which fails against the old guard and passes against the fix (verified both
ways).

Also: bounty_label_of now returns the stripped label on all three branches,
not just the one flagged -- the return value flows into ever_closed_with's
query as label:"{label}", where incidental whitespace would silently fail to
match. And the commaai/opendbc citation (7 closed bounties, no Algora label)
that got dropped when a test was renamed is reattached to
test_keeps_a_repo_that_has_closed_even_one, the test whose mechanism it
actually grounds.

inflection_points.summary: fix: a farm is a repo that never closes a bounty, whatever label it uses
inflection_points.body:
The payout rule only fired on Algora's exact label, so a farm running its own
label was invisible to it. Measured 2026-08-09, zhangjiayang6835-cyber/bounty-plaza
held three of the top four digest slots: 526 open bounties, 0 ever closed, 5
stars, created a month earlier, advertising 'Add a shrimp-person species' at
$200 behind a plain 'Bounty' label.

The label gate is replaced by direct evidence -- has this repo ever CLOSED a
bounty carrying the label it is advertising under. Closed rather than rewarded,
because '💰 Rewarded' is Algora's marker and a repo running its own programme
never sets it: commaai/opendbc has closed seven bounties including a $4,000 port
with no Algora label anywhere.

The lookup costs one search unit per repo per day and is asked only about repos
already over the open-bounty threshold and off the payer roster. It returns None
when it could not look, and every caller abstains on None rather than reading it
as zero.

inflection_points.summary: fix: an Expensify assignee is the reviewer, not the winner
inflection_points.body:
Expensify assigns an internal engineer the moment a job is posted and a C+ when
one volunteers. Verified against the live API on 2026-08-09: #97949 is open and
accepting proposals, labelled External/Daily/Help Wanted, assigned to
stitesExpensify.

So free_reject's blanket assignee rule was rejecting 100% of Expensify
candidates at stage 1 -- the entire \$250 channel, and silently, because a
rejected candidate looks exactly like one that was never posted. It had not
surfaced yet only because the watch cron is hours old and Help Wanted lands about
twice a day.

Whether such a job has actually been awarded is now answered by stage 3: a C+
picks a proposal, its author is assigned and opens the PR, and that is precisely
the claim linked_pr_state tests for.

inflection_points.summary: fix: stop discarding bounties because a bot opened a PR on them
inflection_points.body:
Stage 3 now rejects only when an open linked PR's author is already an assignee,
and scores every other open PR as competition: amount / (1 + comments + 2*prs).
An open PR weighs more than a comment because its author has already written
code, and less than a wall because on Expensify selection is by proposal and on
Algora only a merge wins -- a later entrant may read those PRs and do better.

The 562 candidates already rejected under the old question are cleared at the
start of the run so the new rule actually sees them, and the digest says how many
were re-judged rather than letting a silent revival look like new inventory.

inflection_points.summary: fix: close the check-then-act race in the column migration
inflection_points.body:
_migrate() read PRAGMA table_info and then ran ALTER TABLE with nothing
spanning the check and the write. upsert_candidate's own docstring already
holds this file to a standard here -- two processes sharing the database is
"the normal case, not a corner one" (hunt.py's cron every 3 hours, the
Expensify watch sweep every 10 minutes, independently), measured at 8 of 10
racing writers colliding on a bare check-then-act. On first deploy, while a
database is still on the old schema, two callers of connect() can both see
the column missing before either runs its ALTER, and the loser crashed with
"duplicate column name".

ALTER TABLE now treats that one error string as success: a peer already did
the job this call wanted done. Any other OperationalError -- a genuinely
broken ALTER -- still raises.

Also: added the idempotency test that actually exercises the migrated path
(OLD_SCHEMA -> connect once to run the ALTER -> connect again), since the
existing one only reopened a database that was born on the new schema and
never went through ALTER TABLE at all. And fixed a schema alignment typo:
open_pr_count had two spaces before its type where the rest of the table
uses one.

war_stories.summary: fix: a claimed candidate was stored as never-checked, so it was checked forever
war_stories.body:
Self-review of the TTL two commits back. The claim branch upserted `cand`
before with_linked_prs had been applied, so every candidate rejected as
claimed went into the table with open_pr_count NULL.

Two things wrong with that. Candidate's own docstring defines NULL there as
"the timeline was never read, never that there are no PRs" -- and we had read
it, and found the assignee's own pull request. And recent_pr_check requires a
non-NULL count precisely because a NULL one is not evidence of a check, so
every claimed candidate was re-read on every sweep: the exact per-sweep cost
the TTL exists to remove, left in place for the rows LEAST likely to have
changed, since a bounty already awarded is the one thing that stays awarded.

The test that was supposed to catch this passed for the wrong reason. It
queued no timeline response, so the attempted call raised an unqueued-request
error, which stage 3 caught as an ordinary timeline failure, warned about,
and skipped the upsert for -- leaving the claim standing by accident and the
assertion green. It now asserts no timeline URL was requested at all and that
no timeline warning reached the digest, and was verified red against the old
code before this fix was kept.

The failed-read test was weak in the same way: the candidate had never been
stored at all, so it exercised nothing about the stamp. It now checks a
successfully-stamped row whose TTL has expired, fails the re-read, asserts
the stamp did NOT advance, and asserts the very next sweep asks again rather
than sitting out a fresh six-hour window on the strength of a failure.

war_stories.summary: fix: the staleness rule only ever judged what it had just discovered
war_stories.body:
149f5c0/1d5852d gave the comment ceiling a retroactive half. e785fef gave
the staleness rule none, so a row that went idle AFTER being stored stayed
live indefinitely -- until a source happened to rediscover it, which for a
months-old bounty is never.

The argument is stronger here than for the ceiling, not weaker. A stale issue
is by definition one nothing is happening to, and BountyLabelSource sorts by
`updated` -- so the stalest rows are exactly the ones its pages reach last
and its stop() reaches never. The rule that most needed a retroactive pass
was the only one without one.

store.apply_staleness mirrors apply_comment_ceiling, comparing GitHub's own
timestamp format lexicographically (fixed width, always UTC, so string order
IS chronological). The cutoff is days+1 because free_reject rejects on
`idle > days` and timedelta.days truncates, putting the real line at eight
whole days for STALE_AFTER_DAYS=7; a test pins 7.9 / 8.0 / 8.1 days against
free_reject's own verdict on the same rows, because a rule that keeps a
candidate at stage 1 and rejects it retroactively on the same sweep is worse
than either answer alone. An empty updated_at is skipped rather than swept
up: it sorts before every real timestamp, and "I do not know when" must not
read as "a long time ago".

The reason no longer interpolates the measured idle count. "no activity in
221d" gave every candidate a different spelling of one verdict, and the board
groups its reject table by exact string while clear_rejections matches by
exact string -- so the biggest rule on the board could only ever appear as
dozens of one-row reasons nobody could see the size of or reverse. Both paths
now call filters.stale_reason(), which is also what made writing the SQL half
possible at all: it judges in bulk and has no per-row count to interpolate.

war_stories.summary: fix: two Expensify calls spent more quota than they had reserved
war_stories.body:
The reservation guard is the thing standing between a throttle and a digest
that reports the world as empty (HANDOFF.md trap #3), so a request it has not
counted is a hole in it. Two of them:

_standing reserved ONE search unit and then called search_issues with
max_pages=EXPENSIFY_STANDING_MAX_PAGES (4). Two requests are actually made
today -- 83 results at SEARCH_PER_PAGE 50 -- and the cap is 4 precisely
because that number grows. Every other caller in the tree already reserves up
front: BountyLabelSource reserves self.max_pages, known_payers reserves
`pages`, ever_closed_with reserves 2 for its 2 requests.

The event poll reserved one CORE unit for the whole call, while
poll_label_events' deep-paging block calls _get up to EVENT_MAX_PAGES-1 extra
times. It now reserves the cap when a watermark exists and one when it does
not, because since_event_id is what switches that block on -- reserving five
without a watermark would be spending the guard on requests that cannot
happen. Live as of the previous commit, which is the first time that block
ever ran.

war_stories.summary: fix: silence had come to mean five things, and none of them said which
war_stories.body:
main() passes notify_when_empty=False for both jobs, which is right -- 144
"nothing new" messages a day trains the reader to ignore the channel, so the
one that matters lands somewhere nobody looks. But `flock -n` exits 1 and
prints NOTHING, so Discord silence became indistinguishable between a healthy
quiet market, a hung job holding its lock, a dead box, a lost .env and a
removed crontab. That is the collision this codebase exists to prevent,
reintroduced one layer out.

Two halves, because a log and a channel answer different questions.

The cron jobs now leave a line when they skip. -E 99 and a `[ $? -eq 99 ]`
test rather than a bare `|| echo`: flock passes the command's own exit status
through when it DID get the lock, so the simple form would file every python
traceback as a lock conflict -- one wrong story swapped for another. Verified
locally against a real flock in all three states: lock held writes the line,
lock free does not, and a command exiting 3 does not.

The digest now speaks once every HEARTBEAT_S (24h) regardless, carrying the
sweep count and the live totals. Periodic, not per-run: at ten-minute sweeps
that is 1 message in 144, and the branch is tested against two hours of
sweeps producing exactly two beats rather than twelve. The sweep COUNT is
what makes a half-dead deployment visible -- a heartbeat reading 6 where 144
belong is a watch cron that has stopped, said out loud by the digest cron
that has not.

Stored in http_cache the way board-signature is, and advanced only by a beat
that actually reached someone. A recorded-but-undelivered beat would buy
another full day of silence out of a delivery failure, which is exactly what
it exists to break; --dry-run does not spend it either.

Also corrected the installer's flock preflight comment, which still said both
jobs share one lock. They stopped four commits ago.

war_stories.summary: fix: the deep paging added last commit had never run once
war_stories.body:
poll_help_wanted_events returns events already filtered to `labeled` + Help
Wanted + not-a-PR -- a tiny minority of the feed. The caller then took its
watermark from THAT list, which breaks in both directions and both were live:

  * no matching event yet -> no watermark ever written -> since_event_id
    stays None -> the paging block is skipped entirely. That is the deployed
    state: measured 2026-08-10, the newest Help Wanted label event on
    Expensify/App was three days old, so the feature shipped inert;
  * after one matching event -> the watermark freezes at that id until
    another Help Wanted label lands, so every poll in between re-pages the
    full EVENT_MAX_PAGES (5 core calls, every ten minutes) to re-read pages
    it had already read.

poll_label_events is the only function that sees the unfiltered payload, so
it now returns the newest id ON THE PAGE as a fourth value rather than
leaving the caller to reconstruct it from output it cannot reconstruct it
from. None means the page said nothing -- empty, or a 304 -- and is
deliberately not 0, which is a real id every event compares greater than.

payer-watch unpacks and DISCARDS it, with a note saying why: passing
since_event_id is what turns deep paging on, and that loop runs across up to
WATCH_MAX_REPOS (60) repos a sweep, where one page each is what makes
watching them affordable at all.

Nothing in the suite mentioned since_event_id, watermark or EVENT_MAX_PAGES.
Eleven tests now do, including both failure directions above, the stop at
the page that reaches the watermark, the stop at the cap when it never does,
and the single page read when there is no watermark to page toward.

raw_readme:
# docs/

Hard-won context for the bounty tracker. Written 2026-08-09.

Start with [`../HANDOFF.md`](../HANDOFF.md) — it carries the OPEN ITEMS and the system
overview. These files hold the detail behind it.

| file | what it answers |
|---|---|
| [bounty-market-findings.md](bounty-market-findings.md) | Why the digest is four items long and tuning the filters will not fix it |
| [expensify-proposal-path.md](expensify-proposal-path.md) | Why `has_open_linked_pr()` is wrong for Expensify — an open bug |
| [github-api-traps.md](github-api-traps.md) | Six API behaviours that each silently produced "no bounties" |
| [tracker-operations.md](tracker-operations.md) | What runs where, how to check it is alive, how to intervene |

Every number in these files was measured against the live API, not estimated. Re-verify
before acting on any of them months from now.
